summary:
Farm Forward helps farmers plan crop rotations for a changing climate by showing them where their field's future climate already exists today, and what farmers there grow. We built it after interviewing Jen, a farmer at our local market who told us she's anxious about what climate change means for agriculture. Climate projections arrive as abstract numbers, like "+3 °C by 2060," and a farmer can't easily tell which crops, rotations or risks they mean for their own field. Most climate tools are built for researchers, not for someone setting up a rotation that takes years to play out.

A farmer draws or picks a field on the map and chooses a future: SSP2-4.5 (moderate) or SSP5-8.5 (high emissions). Farm Forward uses 8 NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 climate models to project the field's 2041–2060 climate, then ranks the 20 farm areas whose climate today matches it best, with how many of the 8 models agree. For the closest matches it shows, the rotations farmers there actually grow, re-sorted by the farmer's own priorities: save water, cut erosion, build organic matter, add nitrogen, or break pest and disease cycles; the hazards that come with that climate, from NASA satellites: soil moisture,  ground temperature, heavy rain and bare-soil months, plus hot days and frost dates; a short summary in plain words, whose numbers are checked against the data.

Instead of reading charts, a farmer sees a real place, real rotations and real hazards, and farmers they can learn from.
details:
What it does and how it works
FarmForward shows a farmer where their field's 2050s climate already exists today, and what farmers there grow. The farmer draws their field on a map and picks a scenario, either SSP2-4.5 (moderate) or SSP5-8.5 (high emissions). From there:

  1. PRISM monthly climate for 1995–2014 describes the field today in 8 numbers, average temperature and total precipitation for each season, plus how much they vary from year to year.
  2. Eight NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 climate models project the change from 1995–2014 to 2041–2060. Each model's change is added to the field's real climate to get its 2050s climate.
  3. The tool scores 3,351 farmland cells across the inland Northwest, each about 4.6 km and at least 30% cultivated, using sigma dissimilarity (Mahony et al., 2017). It ranks the best matches and reports how many of the 8 models agree. A score under 1σ is a strong match. A score of 4σ or more triggers a "novel climate" warning.
  4. For the top matches, it reads 2016–2023 USDA Cropland Data Layer labels pixel by pixel to show the rotations those farmers actually grow. The field's current rotation comes first, followed by at least two more options. Each option lists why it was suggested, the evidence, benefits, risks, and gaps.
  5. A hazard outlook compares the field today with the matching place today. It covers hot days and frost dates (PRISM daily), heavy-rain days (NASA GPM IMERG), root-zone soil moisture (NASA SMAP), afternoon ground temperature at 70 m (NASA ECOSTRESS), and bare-field months (Landsat NDVI).
  6. A plain-language summary, a glossary, and a reminder to check with the county extension agent explain the result.

Benefits

  • Abstract climate projections become something a farmer can actually visit and learn from: a real place, real rotations, real hazards.
  • Every number comes from data, and each result says how it was made and what it doesn't know.
  • It's accessible. Units appear in both °C and °F and in both mm and inches, every chart has a screen-reader table, and a plain-words summary is always there.
  • The online demo needs no install.

Intended impact
The goal is to help Palouse dryland farmers plan rotations for soil health and resilience before the climate shifts, not after. In your live runs under SSP2-4.5, every test field's 2050s climate already exists nearby, with strong matches of 0.30–0.49σ that all 8 models agree on. Those places rotate with more fallow, have more hot days, and have a frost-free season about a month longer. For example, Cook Farm at Pullman has 18 hot days a year today, while its best match has 28. That gives farmers and extension agents concrete evidence to discuss. The tool supports the farmer's decision; it doesn't make it.

Tools, languages, and software

  • Backend: Python 3.11 with pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, Pydantic, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Shapely, pyproj, and the Google Earth Engine API.
  • Frontend: TypeScript and React 18 with Vite, Leaflet, react-leaflet, and Leaflet-Geoman. Its types are generated from a shared JSON contract.
  • Testing and deployment: GitHub Actions CI runs 199 backend tests (pytest, ruff) and 60 frontend tests (Vitest) on every pull request. The demo is hosted on GitHub Pages.
  • AI tools: Claude Code helped write the code, tests, and docs under the team's written build rules. Google Gemini optionally writes the plain-language summaries, and every number it writes is checked in code.
  • Data: NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6, GPM IMERG, SMAP, ECOSTRESS, and Landsat 8 and 9, plus PRISM, the USDA Cropland Data Layer, OpenLandMap soils, and SSURGO.
  • Hardware: none. Everything runs in the cloud and in the browser.

How it's creative
Most farm climate tools show charts of projected numbers. FarmForward flips the question: instead of guessing how crops will handle a climate no one has farmed yet, it finds farmers who already farm in that climate and shows what works for them. It combines climate analog mapping with satellite crop histories and NASA hazard data in a way built for a farmer, not a researcher. Gemini only restates results in plain words. It never picks crops or invents numbers.

Factors the team considered

  • Uncertainty: the tool uses 8 models instead of one, offers two emissions scenarios, reports how many models agree, and warns when a field's future climate has no real match today.
  • Honest limits: a crop backtest showed climate alone predicts crop mix only slightly better than random farmland (0.529 vs. 0.517 similarity). Rotations are therefore shown as evidence to discuss, not as predictions.
  • Data fit: candidate cells must be real farmland (at least 30% cultivated). ECOSTRESS readings are split between June, when crops are growing, and July–August, after harvest.
  • The audience: the team used plain language, both unit systems, and screen-reader tables, and points every rotation card to the county extension agent.
  • Trust: every number Gemini writes is checked, a fixed template is used when the check fails, and all matching, rotation, and hazard logic is deterministic code.
  • Quality: each milestone got a self-review, an open-issues list, teach-back questions, and CI.
